title: Belgian Congo
capsule: The Belgian Congo was established in 1908 when the Belgian state took over the Congo Free State, ending the private sovereign rule of King Leopold II, whose regime had become internationally notorious for forced labor, mutilation, and mass death in the rubber concession system. Under Belgian administration the colony of roughly 2.3 million km² was governed as a paternalistic welfare-colonial state combining the administration, Catholic missions, and large mining corporations (notably Union Minière du Haut Katanga), generating vast copper, uranium, and diamond revenues. Nationalist agitation accelerated sharply after 1958; independence was granted on 30 June 1960 as the Republic of the Congo, but the dataset records the colonial period through 1962, encompassing the immediate post-independence crises including the Katanga secession (1960–1963). Belgium's withdrawal was chaotic and contributed directly to the Congo Crisis.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Colonial administrative boundaries are well-documented by Belgian cartographic and administrative records; the 1908–1960 extent is definitively mapped, though internal administrative subdivision boundaries and exact concession-zone limits varied over time and are less precisely rendered in continental-scale datasets.
